An extended series of known standards, given in Table 5 are then run under the same conditions as the samples of interest (gas flow rates, gas species, etc.). These will tend to be offset from the initial calibration baseline by a relatively smooth function, for instance, increasing deviations as a function of melting point. In this way, the actual sample conditions are captured rather than attempting to fit thermal behavior of a particular gas mixture. All of these calibrations are run at a heating rate of 10 K/min. UHP (ultra high purity) argon gas flowing through further in-line gas conditioners is used for both the balance and furnace purge. It should be noted that some reference samples do require caveats relative to their reliability and hence the decision to exclude them from our results. The cobalt and nickel standards severely discolored the crucibles and appeared to wet the crucible to the point of a suspected impurity reaction. Cobalt is typically well suited for a melting point onset but is not reliable for enthalpy of fusion because of rapid sublimation/vaporization. The nickel samples also tended to discolor the alumina with an adherence that also raise some concern about an impurity reaction. Calibration of onset temperatures tends to be relatively straight forward and reliable. There are a few modes of thinking relative to application of the calibration transformation. The curves can be applied to entire blocks of time, that is, from the time after the checks are performed to the time when the next set are performed. Alternatively, if the calibration is assumed to drift systematically, the transformation can be applied by a time-weighted average of the two bounding calibration runs. The temperature data collected here have proven stable enough, differing by no more than 2 degrees between calibration runs, that the errors are assumed to be random rather than systemmatic, and the variation between calibration runs may be useful in capturing the real variation in observation. Further, the deviations in calibration reference runs is lower than the scatter in the observed signals. Therefore, only one transformation encompassing all of the calibration trials is applied to the temperature data recorded in this study.
